description.before: Korea's first walking humanoid (KHR-3), developed at KAIST under Jun-Ho Oh in 2004 and unveiled on January 6, 2005: 125 cm, 56 kg, 66 DoF, 1.25 km/h walk and independently moving five-finger hands. description.after: HUBO is the historical KAIST bipedal research platform at the origin of Rainbow Robotics’ technology lineage. The manufacturer’s heritage describes a 2004 development milestone. Exact original mass, DOF, endurance and first public-release year are not established by the selected heritage account.

description.before: Winner of the DARPA Robotics Challenge Finals 2015 (Team KAIST): disaster-response humanoid that walks upright and rolls on knee-mounted wheels (transformable dual-mode). 175 cm, 80 kg, 32 DoF, BLDC/DC actuators with harmonic reduction gears, 6-axis F/T ankle sensors. Successor of HUBO 2; the lineage continues in Rainbow Robotics platforms.
description.after: DRC-HUBO is the KAIST research humanoid identified by its development institution as the winner of the 2015 DARPA Robotics Challenge. KAIST later documents a HUBO torch-relay demonstration in December 2017. Competition identity and a staged demonstration do not establish a current commercial product, universal disaster-response capability or the legacy row’s exact mechanical specifications.

description.after: RB-Y1 is a wheeled dual-arm research platform introduced publicly in 2024. Official DOF tables disagree within and between documents. Two computers separate real-time control from user applications, with SDK/ROS 2 and simulation interfaces. Grippers, neck modules, cameras and teaching devices depend on configuration; battery energy is not endurance.

highlights: The current RBC family lists ten named six-axis arms with metric payloads from 3 to 30 kg and tabulated reach from 730 to 1900 mm. Exact mounting footprint and robot mass are separate from controller dimensions and weight. In-house reducers, brakes and control technology are manufacturer-positioning claims, not a quantified market-leadership result.

The three named RBC-N arms target food-and-beverage processes with SUS304-based hygienic housing, IP66 and manufacturer NSF/ANSI 169 statements. World-first, safety and certificate claims have not been independently checked; an N name is not interchangeable with a standard arm or a complete cooking cell.

Exact-model protection differs: RB3-730 and RB5-850 tables list IP54; other accessed standard-arm tables list IP66. No model-specific protection rating is assigned to RB16-900 from neighbours. The family-card product query returns the homepage despite HTTP 200, so its missing detail specifications remain unverified.

RB5-850 and RB5-850N narrative reach is 850 mm versus 927.7 mm in their tables/cards. RB5-850 pairs 5 kg with 6.6 lb; RB30-1400 pairs 71 kg with 158 lb. These metric/imperial and narrative/table conflicts stay visible, without choosing a corrected number or inventing a version mapping.

The RBQ-10 page gives conflicting walking speeds (6 versus 9 km/h) and step heights (20 versus 25 cm). Running up to 14 km/h and longitudinal/lateral slopes of 45%/20% retain their mode and percentage units. Two-hour/up-to-four-hour operation has no reviewed workload/configuration conditions.

RBQ-10 exposes LV0/LV1 control and ROS 2/DDS development interfaces; LiDAR, LTE, surveillance modules and wireless charging depend on configuration. Automatic recharge support is separate from charge duration and single-charge endurance.

RBY mobile humanoids, RBM mobile robots, ASTRO application systems and expansion modules appear as adjacent product navigation. Those names do not establish reviewed technical values or create extra robot cards in this arm/quadruped pass. Existing HUBO/FX-2 developer evidence and the RB-Y1 field review remain unchanged.
